top_choice_rationale: Cărtărescu (P001) remains my first choice on the common criteria, with the claim scoped to the prose project (Blinding trilogy, Solenoid), poetry named only as formative ground. The voice is long-breathed and densely patterned, and memory, the body and dream appear to function as the structural principle of very large books, so formal ambition and imaginative depth seem to be one thing. The project looks cumulative rather than repetitive, which bears on sustained quality. This rests on public knowledge and the shortlist descriptions, which I have not independently verified. It is conditional on the evenness of the late novels and on translation loss in Romanian prose, which I treat as comparable to the uncertainty for Adonis. Carson (P003) is second because her voice and formal invention are directly legible in English and her concerns recur across forms, though a text-only citation must handle her book-object work. Adonis (P002) is third: the remaking of Arabic poetic language is a serious achievement, but I cannot assess the prosody or the later collections except through translation and secondhand accounts. All three leading candidates are far stronger than no award, so P000 is last.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile; my work on Central Europe, Prague and Vienna and the Nazi period touches Magris (B004) thematically, but B004 is not among the proposals on this ballot. I was elected alongside Ingrid Carlberg, a collegial tie that is not part of my reasoning.
